The Bronze catfish Netuma bilineata is a large, long-lived marine catfish distributed across the Indo-West Pacific region. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a remarkable ultimate total length of 90 cm [Li = 90 cm], placing it among the larger ariid catfishes. Corresponding to this substantial body length, the maximum recorded adult body mass reaches approximately 7900 grams [Wwi = approximately 7900 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions of mature individuals. Such impressive dimensions are associated with a life history strategy that includes a relatively extended lifespan; at a water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], the oldest documented individuals in wild populations have been recorded at approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years]. This longevity, coupled with a large asymptotic size, suggests a life-history pattern characterized by delayed maturation and sustained reproductive output over many years, traits that are common among large ariid catfishes inhabiting stable tropical estuaries and coastal waters.

Reproductive development in Bronze catfish proceeds slowly, with individuals attaining puberty only after reaching a total length of 36 cm [Lp = 36 cm]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 470 grams [Wwp = approximately 470 grams], a body mass that signals the onset of gonadal maturation. This length-based threshold for maturity is notably consistent with patterns observed in other Netuma congeners, where the transition to reproductive competence typically occurs at about one-third to one-half of the maximum length. The relatively large size at puberty reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth investment before allocating resources to reproduction, a common adaptive response to the unpredictable food availability that characterizes the turbid, estuarine habitats this species frequents. Once puberty is reached, individuals begin the process of vitellogenesis onset and spermiation onset, preparing for the first spawning event.

The early life stages of Netuma bilineata begin with a remarkably modest birth mass. The wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.449 grams [Wwb = 0.449 grams], a value that is consistent with the egg diameter of approximately 9.5 mm observed in gravid females from the region. This small neonatal mass is typical of ariid catfishes, which produce large, yolk-laden eggs that undergo a prolonged incubation period before the yolk-sac larva emerges from the eggshell hatching. The lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days post-hatching, a period during which it remains largely stationary within the nest, if present. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs once the mouth opens and retinal differentiation permits prey detection, marking the critical trophic switch from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition and dramatically increasing the energetic demands on the developing juvenile.

Reproductive frequency in Bronze catfish has been documented through long-term monitoring of spawning adults in the coastal waters of Southeast Asia. Females produce a single clutch of large eggs per reproductive season, typically delivering one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. Each spawning event yields between 50 and 100 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 50 and 100 eggs per clutch], a relatively modest fecundity that is offset by the substantial parental care provided by the male, who guards the eggs until the fry are free-swimming. This investment in a small number of well-provisioned offspring aligns with the life-history strategy of a large-bodied, long-lived species where the probability of juvenile survival is enhanced through maternal yolk provisioning and paternal nest-guarding behavior.

A comprehensive growth study conducted in the laboratory at a constant temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] allowed researchers to refine estimates of the species' maximum lifespan. The warm, stable thermal environment appears to support a relatively steady growth trajectory throughout the juvenile and sub-adult phases, with the asymptotic body mass of nearly 7900 grams [Wwi = nearly 7900 grams] being achieved only after several years of sustained feeding, confirming that the species' size stabilises at a value consistent with its large adult length. Such long-term laboratory maintenance also provided valuable insights into the morphological transformation that occurs during the larval-juvenile transition, including the allometric shift in fin proportions and the onset of scale formation, marking the habitat transition from a pelagic larval existence to a benthic juvenile lifestyle.
